title: Acting in 'The Magic Horn' and 'Show Boat'
summary: He compares acting to playing and describes his roles.

story.theme_name: Radio and television work: staff jobs, shows and broadcasts
story.community_name: Working radio and television: network shows, studio staffs, talk-show bands

blocks.x: Just now when I was indicating from here what an eclectic man you are (LAUGHTER).
Oh good. I'll have to look that up in the dictionary.
One of the things that I mentioned was that you were an actor.
And Sanford says " in those early days on television when so many good shows were originating live as they say in New York. The Alcoa Hour decided on

a script, 'The Magic Horn' which called for an actor trumpet player. Here was a problem. There were trumpet players and there were actors but was there a performer who could act the part believably and play the trumpet loud enough and in the style that was right for the story? There was. It was Jimmy McPartland. And it was good casting. The show came off well and Jimmy played the part so convincingly that his performance drew raving reviews.
"People who were unaware of this side of him were astonished." And I sit here astonished now, so tell me more about this acting. (LAUGHTER).

Well actually, to me it was verbose it was fun, you know. I'm a character at times anyway. I like to talk and it was fun. And I worked quite hard on the thing. I got in good shape physically and excercised, plenty of exercises and studied my lines at home. And I knew the part quite well. And to me it was fun. It was comparable to, in being a musician playing with a band, it's comparable in the acting department for this reason. A musician will know the melody of a tune and the harmonay and you get together with the musicians and you play together and then you get the feeling together and empathy works between you
and the thing starts to swing.

Now with acting, what happened to me, what I felt was once you started acting with an actor and you knew your lines and, as you know the melody as a musician would know it, and you have the feel of the part, why it starts to swing. Actors call it, it starts to play, now it's beginning to play. Now it's starting to play. Or it's playing now. And I found that it was just a lot of fun.

You get swinging and these emotions come out or whatever the part calls for. And the same thing in music comparably. So I do compare the two in that respect and had a lot of fun doing it. I enjoyed it emotionally and as a performer.
And I did play in 'Show Boat' later on too.
Yes, and what role did you play there?
Oh, Shultz, what was my first name? Shultz and Shultz of the well known comedy team and the dance, it's supposed to be a dance....
Song and dance team. (Elly,) I've forgotten even what my first name was. I can't remember.

In the show. But I played Show Boat for Lee (Goobert?) on the Camden, New Jersey Music Fair and the Valley Forge Music Fair for two weeks a piece down there and he wanted to give me more parts but they didn't pay too much money so I figured, I said, I'm going back to that cornet. (LAUGHTER). So I can make some money here, again. (LAUGHTER).
But I really thoroughly enjoyed it because as I say, it is comparable and you have a feel for it. You must have that feel for it I guess like anything else.
